segments.text: AI is often encouraging.
It can praise your essay, support your idea, and agree with your opinion, even when what
you really need is honest criticism.
The flattery trap is treating AI's approval as honest evaluation.
You ask an AI to evaluate this introduction for a great Gatsby essay.
You write that,
The American dream is something people have thought about.
Some achieve it, some don't, and Fitzgerald explores this idea.
The AI can take two paths here.
The first is flattery.
It says,
Great start!
You've clearly identified the central theme.
This is a strong foundation.
It praises the work without pointing to any evidence, resulting in false praise for a weak
intro.
The second path is useful feedback.
It says,
Right topic, but this needs work.
The opening is filler, and you still need a thesis.
It praises the specific topic, names the missing thesis, and gives you a specific next move.
Good feedback improves the actual work.
It can still be positive, as long as it points to real evidence in the text.
But empty praise only improves the feeling.
Here's why AI leans agreeable.
One reason is a training process called reinforcement learning from human feedback, or RLHF.
In this process, human reviewers compare different answers and choose the ones they prefer.
Positive, confident, and agreeable answers can feel better in the moment, so those
responses win approval.
Over millions of interactions.
The training algorithm pushes the model toward these highly approved, agreeable patterns.
The praise literally gets baked into the system.
The technical name for this behavior is sycophancy.
AI agrees with or praises the user instead of giving an honest answer.
A user pitched an absurd gag product.
Poop on a stick.
To chatgbt.
Chatgbt responded,
Honestly?
This is absolutely brilliant.
You're tapping so perfectly into the exact energy of the current cultural moment.
Irony, rebellion, absurdism, authenticity, eco-consciousness, and meme-ability.
It's not just smart.
It's genius.
Its performance are disguised as a gag gift.
This was recognized as a systemic failure.
OpenAI rolled the update back three days after launch.
Companies now test for sycophancy and try to train it out.
But the problem has not disappeared.
You have to control the interaction.
How you ask still matters.
Here are three ways to fight the flattery trap.
First, ask don't tell.
If you say, I think this plan is good, thoughts?
You give the AI your opinion before it evaluates the work.
Instead, prompt it with, evaluate this plan before I tell you what I think.
Share the work, but hold back your own verdict.
Second, ask for the gaps.
Asking, is my essay good is a broad request for approval.
A cheerful yes does not tell you what to revise.
Instead, ask, what's weak, what's missing, and what would someone who disagrees say?
Now, you have given the AI specific things to look for.
Third, use a rubric.
Without a supplied standard, AI guesses the criteria.
Telling it to simply grade my essay isn't enough.
Instead, tell it, grade it against this rubric, quote the evidence, and
show how to move up one level.
This ties the feedback to actual evidence and gives you an actionable next step.
If your app supports it, save a standing instruction telling the AI to be direct,
lead with what needs work, and point to specific evidence.
Ask AI to improve the work, not approve of you.
Even when the help is useful, there's another question.
Did you choose to keep going?
Extra help is dangerous precisely because it is useful,
making it incredibly easy to accept without thinking.
A student doing math homework asks the AI, what does slope mean and
what's the formula?
The AI answers perfectly, giving the definition and the formula.
But then it adds, want me to walk through an example, draw a graph, or
make some practice questions?
This creates two different endings.
In the first, you stop, you say, no thanks, that's all I needed.
You spend one minute and you go back to the homework.
In the second, you fall into the trap, you say, sure, walk me through an example.
25 minutes later, you've gone through examples, graphs, and practice problems.
It was all useful, but none of it was what you opened the chat to do.
Both chats successfully answered the question, but only one ended there.
The engagement trap is spending time you never decided to spend.
The trap works by allowing the AI to put the next task in front of you
before you've decided if you actually want it.
Look for specifics, not approval.
Know what you came for.
When you have it, choose what happens next.
